label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
# Dear Jonno, Since You Asked So Nicely

Mate. You've been messaging me for two weeks asking what happened with the coolroom on Cup Week, so here it is in full. You'd have lost your mind if you'd been here. Probably would've cried too, but you're in London now and apparently that makes you soft, so I'll let you off.

For the record, the compressor died overnight Monday into Tuesday. Nobody knows exactly when. I found out at 6.40am on Cup Day, standing in front of the coolroom door with my keys still in my hand, and the thermometer said 11 degrees. Eleven. That's not a coolroom, that's a bad sandwich shop. And we had 140 covers booked for lunch. Set menu, three courses, the whole Cup Day spiel. Some of those people had hats on, Jonno. Hats.

So first thing, I rang Wally from Coldline. Wally said he couldn't come till Wednesday because the part was coming from Sydney. Sydney. Who orders a compressor part from Sydney? That's not a supply chain, that's a prayer. So it was just me, at 6.45am, with a cold room full of stock slowly turning into a science project.

We moved everything into the two undercounters, the bar fridge, and whatever space we could find. Then Marta from the café next door, bless her, let us use half her walk-in. Which was great, until she made us pay her back in croissant credit. I now owe her about three weeks of staff meal. I've done the maths and I'm going to be eating Marta's pastries until I die.

We still lost about eighteen hundred bucks of stock. Mostly dairy and the duck legs. The duck legs, Jonno. We'd been doing that confit since August. Going into the bin like a dropped pizza. I actually said a small goodbye to them.

Now, head chef Raff was away on Cup Day, which meant I was running the whole thing. Me. Sous. Standing in the middle of the kitchen with a clipboard and a face like a wet weekend, trying to look like I knew what I was doing. Which, fair enough, I did, because you taught me half of it. So blame yourself.

Then the beef shin. Thirty kilos of it, sitting in the one spot that was still cold enough. So me and Benny have to get it from the back of the kitchen down the laneway to Marta's walk-in, which is maybe forty metres, and it's raining. Raining Jonno. Thirty kilos of beef on a milk crate trolley, down a laneway, in the rain. Halfway down one of the wheels fell off. Benny just stood there looking at it like it had personally betrayed him. We ended up sort of dragging the crate the last ten metres with the beef sliding about like it was trying to escape. I'm surprised nobody filmed it. Actually someone probably did and that's the story now.

Dishy Kev, bless him, went and filled the old esky with ice from the servo. Fourteen bags. The servo guy looked at him, looked at the esky, and asked if we were having a party. Kev said, "Sort of." That's the most honest thing anyone said all day.

We had to 86 the panna cotta at 12.15. Panna cotta doesn't set in the time I've got, so dessert became "affogato with whatever." Which, honest opinion, is the best thing that's happened to this restaurant since you left. People loved it more. Some lady said it was the best dessert she's had all year. The panna cotta was never going to get that kind of reaction. Kill your darlings, that's what they say, and apparently I killed the darling and then everyone wanted the stand-in.

And then there's the lady on table nine, who asked our waitress if the beef was "free range from the laneway." Because she'd seen us out the window with the crate. The waitress came back to the pass and said it like she was reporting a crime. "Table nine wants to know if the beef's free range from the laneway." I said yes. Because I'm not going to argue with a woman who's just watched me drag a cow down the street. Would've been rude.

Oh, and I had money on the Cup. My horse was called Ice Cold Lad. Ice Cold Lad. You couldn't make it up. He came second last. The universe is clearly taking the piss, and I'm pretty sure it's doing it on my behalf.

Honestly though, this is the bit I want you to hear. Best service we did all year. Easily. Everyone was locked in. Nobody was trying to be a hero, nobody was precious, everybody just knew what the job was and got on with it. Benny, Kev, the girls on the pass, the waiters who were running between the floor and Marta's cafe with trays of stuff I didn't even know we had. I've been in kitchens for a long time and I've never seen a crew do that. We were down to bar fridges and spite and it still came out clean.

Phil, the owner, came in around eleven, took one look at the chaos and said, "Just make it work, mate." Which, cheers Phil. That's not a plan. That's a vibe. But I'll be honest, we did make it work. Nobody had to be told twice, and it was a proper good day in spite of all the nonsense.

Anyway. That's the story. Eighteen hundred bucks, one dead compressor, one wheel-less crate, fourteen bags of ice, one sad panna cotta, and a lady on nine who thinks we're a farm to table restaurant with a laneway pasture.

So now you know what you've been missing. You're in London, eating overpriced sandwiches and sending me voice notes about how the tube is a nightmare. Meanwhile I'm here, running a bistro on bar fridges, owing Marta half my wages, and getting my horse beaten by a tortoise.

Come home ya flog. The kitchen needs you, the crew needs you, and frankly I need someone to blame for the duck legs.

Love you mate, don't go soft on me.

Aidan
